text:
Today we continue our study in Numbers chapter ten. Israel had now left the wilderness of Sinai. The cloud had lifted from the Tabernacle for the first time after it was erected. The silver trumpets had sounded. The tribes were moving in order. The ark of the covenant was going before them. The journey toward the Promised Land had truly begun. But in the middle of this great movement, the Bible pauses to record a very personal conversation between Moses and a man named Hobab.

Numbers 10:29 says, "And Moses said unto Hobab, the son of Raguel the Midianite, Moses' father in law, We are journeying unto the place of which Yahweh said, I will give it you: come thou with us, and we will do thee good: for Yahweh hath spoken good concerning Israel." Moses looked at Hobab and invited him to join the journey. He did not speak with any uncertainty. He said, "We are journeying unto the place which Yahweh said He will give us." Moses knew that the path through the wilderness would not be easy, but he also knew exactly where the journey was leading. It was leading to the land God had promised. And so Moses said to Hobab, "Come with us, and we will do thee good." It was a beautiful invitation. Moses was inviting Hobab to walk with Israel and to share in the goodness that God had spoken concerning His people.

But Hobab's first answer was not yes. Numbers 10:30 says, "And he said unto him, I will not go; but I will depart to mine own land, and to my kindred." Hobab wanted to return to his own land and to his own family. This was natural. The wilderness journey was uncertain. Israel was moving toward a place they had not yet seen. Hobab may have thought it safer to return to what he already knew. His people, his land, and his familiar life lay behind him.

The journey with Israel required faith. But Moses did not give up. Numbers 10:31 says, " Please don't leave us," Moses pleaded. "You know the places in the wilderness where we should camp. Come, be our guide." Moses pleaded with him, "Please do not leave us." Then he gave the reason. Hobab knew the wilderness. He knew the camping places. He knew the desert paths. He knew the difficult places where water, shade, grazing, and safety could be found. Moses said, "You may be to us instead of eyes."
This does not mean that Moses did not trust the cloud. The cloud was still the true guide of Israel. Yahweh was leading them from above. But Hobab had practical knowledge of the wilderness below. The cloud showed when to move and when to stop, but Hobab could help the people understand the ground, the valleys, the watering places, and the dangers of the desert. Moses then added one more promise. Numbers 10:32 says, " If you do, we'll share with you all the blessings Yahweh gives us.." Moses was saying, "If you come with us, whatever goodness Yahweh gives to us, we will share it with you." This was not only an invitation to travel. It was an invitation to share in the very blessing that had been promised to Israel.

Now the question rises, who exactly was Hobab? Hobab was a Midianite from the family of Moses' wife. Numbers 10:29 calls him the son of Raguel, or Reuel, the Midianite. Reuel is also connected with Moses' father-in-law in Exodus 2:18. In other places, Moses' father-in-law is called Jethro. Because thier family terms can sometimes be used broadly, there is some discussion about the exact relationship. But the simple understanding is that Hobab belonged to Moses' Midianite in-law family, and many understand him to be Moses' brother-in-law. Moses had lived in Midian for about forty years before returning to Egypt. During that time he married Zipporah, the daughter of Jethro. So Moses knew this family very well. Hobab was not a stranger to him. He was connected to him through family. Yet he was not an Israelite by birth. He was a Midianite. This makes the invitation even more meaningful. Hobab was being invited to leave his own land and journey with the people of Yahweh, and to share in the promise Yahweh had spoken concerning Israel.

The Bible does not immediately say in Numbers ten, "Hobab went with them." But the later Scriptures strongly show that his family did indeed join themselves to Israel. In Judges 1:16 we read, "And the children of the Kenite, Moses' father in law, went up out of the city of palm trees with the children of Judah into the wilderness of Judah." This verse shows that the family connected to Moses' in-laws later lived among Israel, especially with the tribe of Judah. They became known as the Kenites. They were not one of the twelve tribes by birth, but they attached themselves to Israel and became part of Israel's story. This appears to be the very fruit of Moses' invitation. Hobab may have hesitated at first, but his family line became joined to the people of Yahweh. Moses said, "Come with us," and generations later we see his descendants living among Judah.

Judges 4:11 gives us another important detail. It says, "Now Heber the Kenite was of the children of Hobab the father in law of Moses." This connects Hobab's descendants with the Kenites, and it brings us to one of the most remarkable women in the book of Judges: Jael. In Judges chapter four, Israel was oppressed by Jabin king of Canaan. Sisera, the commander of Jabin's army, had nine hundred chariots of iron, and he oppressed Israel greatly. Yahweh raised up Deborah and Barak to deliver His people. During the battle, Sisera fled and came to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite. Jael welcomed Sisera into the tent. He asked for water, and she gave him milk. He lay down, exhausted, and fell asleep. Then Jael took a tent peg and a hammer and killed Sisera, and by her hand Yahweh brought down the enemy of Israel. This is very powerful. From the very family line that Moses invited to join Israel came Jael, a woman who helped to deliver Israel from oppression. The family that was invited to share Israel's blessings later became a blessing to Israel.

The Kenites continued to appear later in Israel's history. In 1 Samuel 15:6, when Saul was about to strike Amalek, he warned the Kenites to leave the Amalekites so that they would not be destroyed with them. Saul said, "Go, depart, get you down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them: for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel, when they came up out of Egypt."

This shows that the kindness of the Kenites was remembered generations later. They had shown kindness to Israel, and now Israel showed mercy to them. Moses had promised Hobab that Israel would do him good, and we see that goodness continuing on through history. There is also further connection between the Kenites and the Rechabites. In 1 Chronicles 2:55 we read of "the Kenites that came of Hemath, the father of the house of Rechab." Later, in Jeremiah chapter thirty-five, the Rechabites are presented as a people who obeyed the command of their father Jonadab. They refused wine and lived according to the instruction passed down to them, and Yahweh used their obedience as a lesson to Judah, because the Rechabites obeyed their father's command while Judah had not obeyed Yahweh's voice. The family line related to Hobab continued as a separated and obedient people for many generations. They were not originally Israelites by blood, yet they became connected with Israel's God, Israel's land, and Israel's history.
This is a beautiful history. Hobab's story begins with an invitation: "Come with us." It continues with hesitation: "I will not go." Then Moses pleads with him again and says, "Please do not leave us." He reminds Hobab that he can be useful in the wilderness journey, and he promises that the goodness Yahweh gives to Israel will also be shared with him. From that single invitation, we later see a family connected to Hobab living among Judah. We see Jael, from the Kenite line, gaining the victory over Sisera. We see the Kenites remembered in Saul's day for their kindness. And we may even see their line connected with the Rechabites, who were praised for their obedience in the days of Jeremiah. So the words of Moses were not empty words. "Come with us, and we will do thee good" became a doorway into a long history of blessing, service, kindness, and obedience; a history that stretched across many generations of Israel's walk with Yahweh. There are many deep lessons hidden in this passage; Moses inviting Hobab, Hobab's first refusal, Moses pleading again, the promise to share Israel's blessing, Hobab's family becoming joined to Judah, Jael's victory over Sisera, the kindness remembered in Saul's day, and the Rechabites.

The lesson for the New Creation from this beautiful history, God willing, we will study in tomorrow's Morning Light.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,

We thank You for the beautiful history hidden in a single conversation in the wilderness.

Moses said, 'Come with us, and we will do thee good,' and the words did not fall to the ground;

they opened a doorway of blessing that reached across many generations.

We thank You that Your goodness spoken over Your people always proves true.

Help us to believe Your promises as Moses believed them, without wavering.

And let the kindness shown among Your people be remembered and rewarded by You.

" Great is Yahweh, and greatly to be praised; and His greatness is unsearchable."- Psalm 145:3

In Christ name we pray. Amen.
